title: History of Food, Food Preservation and Traditional Foods
shortDescription: From fire and fermentation to canning and irradiation — plus why traditional Indian foods still matter.
genZNote: Your pickle is a 5,000-year-old science experiment that actually worked. History of food = history of 'how do we stop this from rotting?'

sections.heading: Milestones in Food and Preservation
sections.body: Preservation always attacks one or more of: microbial growth, enzyme activity, chemical (oxidative) change and pest damage — via heat, cold, water removal, acidity, salt/sugar, smoke, chemicals or irradiation.

table.caption: Timeline
rows: Agriculture and animal domestication; storage in pits and pots
Fermentation (bread, beer, curd, soy), pickling, honey and oil preservation
Nicolas Appert: heat-processing food in sealed glass bottles; Napoleon's prize
Louis Pasteur: microbes cause spoilage; pasteurization
Mechanical refrigeration; commercial freezing (Clarence Birdseye, 1920s quick-freezing)
HACCP (NASA/Pillsbury, 1960s), irradiation, aseptic packaging, modified atmosphere
High-pressure processing, pulsed electric fields, cold plasma, precision fermentation

sections.heading: Traditional Foods and Why They Matter
bullets: Fermented staples (idli, dosa, dhokla, dahi, kanji, handia, kimchi analogues) improve digestibility, B-vitamin content and shelf life, and carry beneficial microbes.

Millets (jowar, bajra, ragi — "Shree Anna"), pulses, ghee, jaggery, turmeric, local leafy greens: nutrient-dense, climate-resilient, low glycaemic load when unrefined. 2023 was the International Year of Millets (proposed by India).
Preservation traditions: sun-drying (papad, vadi), pickling (achar), salting, sugar syrups (murabba), smoking, oil-sealing.
Traditional processing also shows nutrient science: soaking/sprouting reduce phytates and raise bioavailability; combining cereal + pulse improves protein quality (complementary amino acids).
Regional Gujarati examples: thepla, khichdi–kadhi, dhokla, khakhra, undhiyu, handvo — fermented/dry foods suited to long storage and travel.

sections.heading: Protecting Food Heritage
sections.body: Geographical Indication (GI) tags (Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999), FSSAI's "Eat Right" and local-food promotion, and recognition of traditional knowledge protect authenticity and livelihoods; but traditional foods still need modern hygiene (GHP) to be safe.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: Food preservation evolved from drying, salting and fermentation to heat-processing, refrigeration and non-thermal technologies, while traditional foods offer nutrition, sustainability and cultural value.
keyFacts: Appert (1795–1810) founded canning; Durand patented the tin can.
Fermentation improves digestibility, vitamins and keeping quality.

commonTraps: Do not credit Pasteur with inventing canning.

questions.prompt: Who is regarded as the father of canning?
questions.explanation: Appert showed heat-sealed food in bottles could be preserved.

questions.prompt: International Year of Millets was observed in:
questions.explanation: The UN declared 2023, proposed by India.

questions.prompt: Soaking and sprouting of pulses mainly help by:
questions.explanation: They reduce phytates and improve mineral availability.
